title: Constantinople III, 681
hookLine: Christ has a truly human will as well as a divine one

cards: A garden at night, across the valley from Jerusalem.

Jesus has gone a little apart from his friends, and Luke's Gospel says he kneels and prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." Read it slowly.
There is a will that would rather the cup pass, and there is a yes. Long afterward, bishops argued over that one sentence, because it holds a question: when Jesus says my will, whose will is that?
The answer came from the council called Constantinople the Third.

teach.b: After Chalcedon said Christ has two natures, some tried a middle road to bring divided churches back together.
Fine, they said, two natures, but only one will: the divine will doing all the willing, the humanity just carried along. It sounded peaceful. Others saw the cost.
Gregory of Nazianzus had put the principle long before: what Christ did not take on, he did not heal.

teach.h: MAXIMUS: NOT FULLY HUMAN WITHOUT IT.
teach.b: A monk remembered as Maximus the Confessor argued that a human nature without a human will isn't fully human, and tradition says he paid dearly for saying so.

The Catechism gives the council's answer: at the sixth ecumenical council, Constantinople III, in 681, the Church confessed that Christ has two wills and two natural operations, divine and human. And they are not opposed.

teach.h: NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.
teach.b: His human will does not resist his divine will; it follows it, submits to it. Go back to the garden. Not my will, but thine.
As the council's defenders saw it, if Jesus had no human will, there would be nothing to surrender, and those words would be play-acting.
Because he does, the garden is real: a real human wanting, a real dread of the cup, and a real human yes, given freely to the Father.
On this reading, Christ knows from inside what it costs to say yes when everything in you leans the other way. A human will. Not crushed, not erased, but given.

how: Catholics pray Thy will be done in the Our Father and meditate on Christ's prayer in Gethsemane in the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden.

o: the council that said Christ has a human will too
the third time the emperor's capital was besieged
a third creed written for the city's churches

p: the middle road the council rejected
not fully human without a human will

s: the council said Christ had only a divine will
it confessed two wills, divine and human.
Christ's two wills fight each other
the Catechism says they are not opposed; the human will follows the divine.
in the garden Jesus asks for the chalice to be removed
and then: not my will, but thine be done.

games.q: you're a bishop. one will in Christ would bring divided churches back together. it sounds peaceful. what do you say?
o: accept it for the sake of peace.
say Christ has a human will too, or he isn't fully human.
games.why: the council confessed two wills, divine and human, not opposed: the human will freely following the divine.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you want today that you may not get, a result, an apology, an easy afternoon, and name it honestly, the way the garden prayer does.
Then see if there's a little room to open your hands around it: not to stop wanting, just to loosen your grip.
If you pray, say Jesus's words from the garden, not my will, but thine be done; if you don't, simply breathe out with open hands.

wordCard.voice: Constantinople III. The sixth ecumenical council, which confessed that Christ has a truly human will as well as a divine one, never opposed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a human will. Tomorrow, the icons come back to Nicaea. Day seven hundred seventy-four, done.
